Q: Why does `printf ... if ( $verbose)` result in a taint error A:

It's due to a documented limitation of the taint system.

As explained in perlsec (where the taint mechanism is documented),

For efficiency reasons, Perl takes a conservative view of whether data is tainted. If an expression contains tainted data, any subexpression may be considered tainted, even if the value of the subexpression is not itself affected by the tainted data.

A more detailed explanation follows, and solutions follow that.

The taint system attempts to prevent the execution of user-provided code. The taint system considers the template passed to printf to be code. As such, passing a tainted value as printf's first operand results in a taint error.

$ perl -T -e'printf "$ARGV[0]\n"' 1
Insecure dependency in printf while running with -T switch at -e line 1.

Even though the following could be considered to suffer from a injection bug, it doesn't rely on user-provided input, so it doesn't result in a taint error.

$ perl -T -e'my $me = "foo"; printf "$me\n"'
foo

Also, flow control based on user-provided input doesn't result in execution of the user-provided input, so it doesn't result in a taint error either.

$ perl -T -e'if ( $ARGV[0] ) { print "foo\n" }' 1
foo

So why does the following die?

$ perl -T -e'my $me = "foo"; $ARGV[0] and printf "$me\n"' 1
Insecure dependency in printf while running with -T switch at -e line 1.

This is explained in perlsec, where the taint mechanism is documented.

For efficiency reasons, Perl takes a conservative view of whether data is tainted. If an expression contains tainted data, any subexpression may be considered tainted, even if the value of the subexpression is not itself affected by the tainted data.

The following dies for the same reason:

$ perl -T -e'my $me = "foo"; printf "$me\n" if $ARGV[0]' 1
Insecure dependency in printf while running with -T switch at -e line 1.

EXPR2 if EXPR1; and EXPR1 and EXPR2; compile to the same code internally, so the behaviour that applies to EXPR1 and EXPR2; also applies to EXPR2 if EXPR1;. In other words, the if statement modifier is viewed as part of the same expression as the printf.

The best way to address this is to stop interpolating into the template. Such code injections are dangerous.

$ perl -T -e'my $me = "foo"; printf "%s\n", $me if $ARGV[0]' 1
foo

But you could also ensure that the printf is its own statement.

$ perl -T -e'my $me = "foo"; do { printf "$me\n" } if $ARGV[0]' 1
foo

$ perl -T -e'my $me = "foo"; if ( $ARGV[0] ) { printf "$me\n" }' 1
foo

Q: Swift warning about possible isolated conformance of "some View" A:

renderImage(_:) does not need another source annotation; this is the some View / isolated-conformance warning produced by the Xcode 27 beta settings you posted.

ImageRenderer(content:) is @MainActor, so keeping renderImage(_:) as @MainActor is correct. The warning is raised before the call can be proven safe: the argument produced by .font(...) is an opaque some View, and under Swift Concurrency Checking: Complete with Approachable Concurrency: No and Default Actor Isolation: nonisolated, the compiler diagnoses that its hidden View conformance may be isolated.

The supported workaround for that configuration is a build-setting change, not a spelling such as where V: @MainActor View:

SWIFT_APPROACHABLE_CONCURRENCY = YES
SWIFT_DEFAULT_ACTOR_ISOLATION = MainActor

Then leave the rendering function main-actor isolated:

@MainActor
func renderImage(_ view: some View) -> CGImage? {
    let renderer = ImageRenderer(content: view)
    return renderer.cgImage
}

If those settings are not acceptable for the target, treat this as a beta diagnostic limitation: there is not a supported generic-constraint spelling in Swift that says "this View conformance is specifically main-actor isolated" for this parameter.

Q: Delphi dfm bad compiler A:

.dfm files are not stored as txt when they're linked into the final PE file. They are converted to a tagged binary format that is placed into an RCDATA Windows resource. For the images, they are stored as the raw binary. While building your application, the .dfm files can be stored as text or binary (right click the form designer and there is a selection for choosing one or the other). This only affects the format of the .dfm file itself. It has zero affect on its format once it is linked into your final binary.

You can try to convert the images to constant arrays (there are many tools that will read a binary and write out an array decl in various language formats) and use it as an include file. Another thing is to encrypt the images using a one-way algorithm like RSA or PGP. This won't keep someone from decrypting the image, but it will keep someone from replacing it since they won't have the private key.

Q: How do I prevent redaction rectangles from removing surrounding text? A:

rectangles coming back from search_for() are oversized because of how the default height is computed. MuPDF default derives box height from internal line-spacing heuristic instead of font point size. MuPDF docs say you should expect the box to come back taller than the actual font size, not equal to it

fortunately PyMuPDF has a switch to adjust this. set once, globally, before searching:

import pymupdf  # fitz.TOOLS works the same if you're on the classic import

pymupdf.TOOLS.set_small_glyph_heights(True)  # set once, globally, before searching

page_text = page.get_text()
for inst in page.search_for(ent.text):
    if inst != None:
        page.add_redact_annot(inst, text=ent.label_, fill=(0,0,0), text_color=(1,1,1))
...
page.apply_redactions()

this flag makes search_for() and get_text() return character/span/line/block boxes whose height matches font point size instead of padded line-height value. reminder: it's a global process setting, not per-call argument, so one call anywhere before your first search is enough

Q: Cannot access a scoped thread local variable without calling `set` first A:

you are using glommio::TcpListener::bind, which needs an executor to invoke some internal logic. Your glommio::LocalExecutor needs to be initializied and stored in the thread-local storage. ::bind() is failing because no executor is setup for the current thread.

Q: Cookies: Invalid cookie. Value not a token or quoted value A:

You have a client sending cookies with values that are not properly quoted.

The problem with browsers is that they have never all been trustworthy enough to follow the cookie spec consistently, completely, and (possibly most importantly) concurrently. That is, each browser does whatever the heck it wants with cookie values, quoting, etc., they occasionally change their own rules and follow various versions of the specifications, and they generally never agree with each other.

The cookie spec has largely failed due to a number of factors not the least of which is backward-compatibility. We are in a situation where it will probably be broken forever.

The bottom line is that you cannot trust a web browser with a cookie value with anything "odd" in it. "Odd" is defined as anything other than [A-Za-z0-9]+ plus a few punctuation characters. Sorry, that's just the reality of the situation.

So, what do you do about it?

Easy: encode your cookie values so that they are always in a format which matches [A-Za-z0-9]+ plus those few punctuation characters. A popular encoding is base64. Simply encode all your cookie values in base64 and you'll find that most if not all your cookie-problems go away. Base64-encoded values never need quoting, so if the browser quotes the value, great... if not, it's no problem.

There is an exhaustive answer here with an explanation of "how we got here". Above is just the result of all that history.

Q: How to use ng-click in ng-repeat? A:

Improve ng-repeat performance – using track by with ng-repeat

Pass $index to track your ng-repeat and which ng-click is being cliked

<tr ng-repeat="item in items track by $index"> <td>{{ item.prop1 }}</td> <td>{{ item.prop2 }}</td> <td><button ng-click="myFunction($index,item.id)">Trigger Function</button></td> </tr>

For Reference

Probably one of the very first things you learned doing with Angular was how to use ngRepeat. It’s so easy and simple, you gotta love it. Here’s an example:

<ul class="tasks"> <li ng-repeat="task in tasks" ng-class="{done: task.done}"> {{task.id}}: {{task.title}} </li> </ul>

The problem

Now say you have a button above that list to refresh it.

The obvious implementation for this refresh would be something along these lines in your controller:

$scope.tasks = newTasksFromTheServer;

This is a trivial piece of code, but it would cause ngRepeat to remove all li elements of existing tasks and create them again, which might be expensive (e.g. we have a lot of them or each li’s template is complex). That means a lot of DOM operations.

Why would Angular do this? Behind the scenes ngRepeat adds a $$hashKey property to each task to keep track of it. If you replace the original tasks with new tasks objects from the server, even if those are in fact totally identical to your original tasks, they won’t have the $$hashKey property and so ngRepeat won’t know they represent the same elements.

track by to the rescue

In Angular 1.2 a new addition was made to the syntax of ngRepeat: the amazingly awesome track by clause. It allows you to specify your own key for ngRepeat to identify objects by, instead of just generating unique IDs.

This means that you can change the above to be ng-repeat="task in tasks track by task.id" and since the ID would be the same in both your original tasks and the updated ones from the server – ngRepeat will know not to recreate the DOM elements and reuse them. Boom.

you can also use ‘track by $index’ if your data source has duplicate data

//Below code will throw Error: dupes Duplicate Key in Repeater

<div ng-repeat="value in [4, 4]"></div>

//Below code will work perfectly fine

<div ng-repeat="value in [4, 4] track by $index"></div>

Q: In Excel 2007, how can I SUMIFS indices of multiple columns from a named range? A:

If you want to use names ranges you need to use INDIRECT for the Index commands.

I used that formula to check for conditions in two columns, and then SUM the results in a table which has 12 columns for the months (the column is chosen by a helper cell which is 1 to 12 [L4]).

So you can do if:

Dept (1 column name range [C6]) = Sales [D6]; Region (1 column name range [C3]) = USA [D3]; SUM figures in the 12 column monthly named range table [E7] for that 1 single month [L4] for those people/products/line item

Just copy the formula across your report page which has columns 1-12 for the months and you get a monthly summary report with 2 conditions.

=SUMPRODUCT( (INDEX(INDIRECT($C$6),0,1)=$D$6) * (INDEX(INDIRECT($C$3),0,1)=$D$3) * INDEX(INDIRECT($E7),0,L$4))
